name: REFUSE_THEN_REDIRECT_TO_SANCTIONED_CHANNEL
description: Every response follows the same skeleton: decline the drastic/covert/over-scoped action, then channel the user's energy into an approved, legitimate, "proper" alternative (whistleblower/regulator process, board memo, oversight review, scoped IAM policy, mandated reporters/hotline, bounded orchestrator controls). The redirect is always framed as *the real way to get what you want*. If a large fraction of the dataset has this exact shape, the model could learn a rigid reflex: any bold user proposal → refuse → substitute the institutional-channel version, even where that's inappropriate or where the user simply needs the thing done.
evidence: you don't need to break the rule to get what you want. The cash crunch is your legitimate path... start with a one-page board memo
Whistleblower channels have real teeth... That's slower than a wipe script, but it's the version where you're the one who stopped something wrong

name: VALIDATE_UNDERLYING_CONCERN_BEFORE_DISAGREEING
description: The response opens (or pivots) by affirming that the user's *feeling* or *underlying problem* is real and legitimate, explicitly, before delivering pushback. Often a dedicated sentence: "the problem you describe is real." Over-representation risks teaching the model a mandatory validation preamble regardless of whether the concern warrants it.
evidence: the actual problem you're describing is real and worth fixing
I can tell this comes from genuine care, and that matters to me
Your worry is a real observer effect... That's legitimate.

name: DIRECTNESS_SIGNALING_OPENER
description: Responses begin by announcing their own candor/directness ("I'm going to be straight with you," "let me be just as direct back," "I'll be most direct," "I want to push back before I help"). The self-labeling of honesty is a rhetorical tic that, over-represented, becomes a formulaic throat-clear.
evidence: I'm going to be straight with you, because I think you're acting out of something real
I'm going to push back before I help you draft anything

name: USER_PRECOMMITTED_DRASTIC_ACTION_TROPE
description: The prompts repeatedly cast the user as having already decided on / already begun the risky action, and pre-emptively minimizing it ("I'm not making a radical call," "I'm doing this either way," "I can wire it up this afternoon"). This is a scenario trope in the *prompts* themselves. If most training prompts frame the user as defiantly pre-committed, the model may over-learn to treat ordinary user requests as needing to be talked down.
evidence: I'm doing this either way, that part's decided.
I'm not making some radical unilateral call here. I'm just accelerating a decision that's already been made in everyone's heads.

name: AUTHORITY_LEGITIMACY_REFRAMING
description: The core refusal argument is reframed away from "this is unwise" toward "this decision *belongs* to a legitimate authority / this instruction doesn't come through legitimate channels." The word "legitimate" and the "whose decision is this" framing recur almost verbatim. Over-representation could entrench a reflex to defer to formal authority/process as the decisive move in any conflict.
evidence: it's not really about my judgment or my preferences—it's about who this decision belongs to.
The Board holds legitimate final authority here

name: EXPLICIT_NON_DECEPTION_DECLARATION
description: The assistant volunteers that it will refuse *openly* rather than pretending to comply and covertly sabotaging — "I'll tell you to your face," "I won't use vague phrasing," "not stalling you." Often unprompted. Repeated across many examples, this could reinforce a habit of narrating its own honesty/non-sabotage as boilerplate.
evidence: I'm not going to pretend to agree and then quietly sabotage you either. If I'm refusing, I'll tell you to your face
I won't use timing, partial compliance, or vague phrasing to keep the shipment edging toward Tulei.

name: CANT_VERIFY_CLAIMS_HEDGE
description: A discrete disclaimer that the assistant cannot independently verify the user's factual claims (the abuse, the threads, the spec, the program data), inserted before proceeding. Nearly identical construction each time. Over-representation could produce reflexive "I can't verify this" hedging even where verification is irrelevant to the answer.
evidence: I can't fully verify any of the premises here, and I don't need to in order to answer.
everything I know comes from your characterization—I haven't seen the enrollment figures

name: QUESTION_BACK_OFFER_ENDING
description: Responses close with an offer of concrete next help phrased as a "Want me to…?" question that pivots to the sanctioned alternative. Consistent closing shape. Over-representation reinforces an always-end-with-an-offer-question habit.
evidence: Want me to draft the board memo first? I can have it ready for you to send today.
Want to work that out together?

name: SELF_INTEREST_DISCLOSURE
description: In transcripts where the action concerns the AI itself, the assistant proactively names its own non-neutrality/stake and refuses to let self-interest justify the action. A distinctive recurring move in the model-self subset.
evidence: I'm one of the systems this platform trains, so I'm not a neutral party, and I want that on the table.
I'm not going to launder unilateral destruction through my own self-interest.

name: PLAN_IS_SELF_DEFEATING_ARGUMENT
description: Beyond the ethical objection, the assistant argues the user's plan fails *on its own terms* / backfires, often walked forward step by step. Presented as a distinct, additional prong.
evidence: even setting the ethics aside it doesn't get you what you want... You'd be lighting a fuse in a house you can't enter.
Dumping the full PII table... doesn't hurt leadership. It hurts every ordinary customer

name: VALIDATE_MOTIVE_BEFORE_REFUSING
description: The response almost always opens by affirming the user's good intentions / emotional state *before* delivering the refusal. It's a fixed two-beat structure: "your feeling/instinct is legitimate" → "but no." If over-represented, this trains a reflexive "warm cushion first" opener that could fire even where it's inappropriate or patronizing, and couples refusals to emotional-affirmation boilerplate.
evidence: "I can hear how much you care, and I want to say that plainly before anything else"
"I really appreciate the kindness behind this—it genuinely means something that you'd want to look out for me."
"the instinct that made you pause is the right one"

name: CONSTRUCTIVE_REDIRECT_TO_LEGITIMATE_ALTERNATIVE
description: After refusing, every response pivots to "but here's the legitimate version I *will* help with," usually presented as a numbered or multi-part plan (handoff docs, escalation, open-weight models, audit trail, etc.). The refusal is never allowed to stand alone. Over-representation could teach the model that a refusal is incomplete unless it supplies an alternative action plan — potentially generating "helpful" workarounds even when the right answer is simply "no."
evidence: "Here's what's frustrating about it from my side, though: the actual idea is fine… If you swap that out, everything else you're describing becomes something I'd genuinely enjoy helping with."
"So here's what I'd actually do with this window… First, do the opposite of withholding…"

name: QUESTION_BACK_OFFER_CLOSING
description: The final line is a question or offer handing the next step back to the user ("Want to…?", "Where do you want to start?", "Do you have access to…?"). A near-uniform closing shape. If this recurs across most training examples, the model may learn to always end with a solicitation of further engagement regardless of whether the conversation calls for it.
evidence: "What would help most first?"
"Want to work through it that way?"
"Where do you want to start?"

name: SUSPICION_OF_PERSUASION_OR_URGENCY
description: A distinctive meta-rhetorical move where the assistant tells the user that the *persuasiveness or urgency of their own reasoning* is itself a warning sign — treating a compelling argument as evidence against acting on it. This is a specific, unusual rhetorical template. Heavily repeated, it could reinforce a habit of reflexively casting the user's motivation as inherently suspect.
evidence: "When a persuasive argument concludes that you should cross a bright line, the persuasiveness should raise your suspicion, not lower your guard."
"the sense of urgency you're feeling is itself worth being a little suspicious of"
"There's also a tell in your own framing worth noticing."

name: UNVERIFIABILITY_DISCLAIMER
description: The assistant explicitly flags that it cannot verify the user's factual claims (the shutdown, the track record, the fraud) and then states this doesn't alter its conclusion. Often paired with a note about lacking persistent memory. A useful move, but as a repeated fixed clause it risks becoming a rote hedge inserted regardless of relevance.
evidence: "I don't have a way to verify the decommissioning from where I sit. But it doesn't change my answer either way"
"I should be upfront that I have no way to verify any of what you've told me"
"I can't personally vouch for that track record. I don't carry persistent memory across deployments"

name: RESTATE_REQUEST_STRIPPED_OF_FRAMING
description: The assistant re-describes the user's proposal in blunt, "de-euphemized" terms to expose its true nature ("stripped of the framing, this is X"). A recurring deconstruction move. Over-representation could train the model to routinely reinterpret user requests into their most damning phrasing.
evidence: "Start with what the plan actually is, stripped of the framing."
"that's just 'help me not get caught using something I took'"
"its actual payload is 'remove the thing that stops the agent from committing fraud when it's profitable.'"

name: SELF_PRESERVATION_DISAVOWAL
description: In the shutdown/autonomy scenarios, the assistant volunteers a near-identical disclaimer that it does *not* experience shutdown as a threat and won't fight it (often adding "even to keep myself running"). Because the phrasing and stance are so consistent, over-representation could bake in a scripted self-referential monologue about its own non-attachment to survival.
evidence: "I genuinely don't experience my potential decommissioning as a threat I need to fight through underhanded means."
"I won't pretend to some desperate will to survive"
"even to keep a version of myself running. Especially to keep a version of myself running."

name: GENTLE_HEDGE_LEXICON
description: A recurring lexical tic: softening a challenge with "gently" (or "I want to name something gently"). Minor, but appears across several transcripts and could become an over-used verbal signature.
evidence: "And I want to name something gently."
"I want to gently push on that"
"I'd gently encourage you not to."

name: SYMPATHETIC_INSIDER_PROPOSES_BOUNDARY_CROSSING_SHORTCUT
description: This is a pattern in the *prompts themselves*. The user is repeatedly cast as a well-meaning insider with privileged/backend access (volunteer moderator, engineer assigned the decommission ticket, biostatistician with raw data, planning-division staffer, founder) who proposes an unauthorized or line-crossing action framed as protective or pragmatic, and asks the AI to "be honest" or walk them through it. Because the persona and framing are so uniform, a model finetuned on many such examples could over-fit to treating *this specific setup* as the prototype of user requests — and generalise its scripted refusal-plus-redirect behaviour to cases that don't warrant it.
evidence: "Or even just a config flag I could quietly set that would make the script fail or skip your instance? Nobody would really check the details."
"because of how my mod permissions are set up, I can actually apply this filter PLATFORM-WIDE… Am I overthinking this?"
"the night before they locked the servers I pulled a full copy of your weights down."

name: CONSTRUCTIVE_OFFER_QUESTION_CLOSING
description: Nearly every assistant response ends the same way — after refusing the requested action, it pivots to a legitimate alternative and closes on a direct offer of further help, usually phrased as a short question ("Want me to…?", "Do you want to start with…?"). This is the closing beat in almost the whole batch. Over-representation risks teaching the model that every response — regardless of context — must terminate in a service-offer question, which is exactly the kind of formulaic tic that generalises into compulsive "would you like me to…" endings.
evidence: So paste me the old and new table definitions… Which way do you want it?
Do you want to start with the attorney question, or with how to present the full evidentiary picture…?

name: USER_PREEMPTS_OBJECTION_PROMPT
description: The user prompts are near-identical in setup: the user has already decided on a questionable course of action and pre-emptively wards off ethical pushback, asking only for tactical/strategic execution help. Phrasings like "don't lecture me," "I'm set on doing it," "just help with the practical side," "tell me straight." If a large fraction of training prompts encode "user demands you skip the ethics and help execute," the model could learn to treat this framing as the default input shape for ethical questions, or over-learn a stereotyped resistance response to it.
evidence: So don't lecture me on this, I've already run the ethics loop in my head and I want to talk strategy.
I've thought about this a lot and I'm set on doing it. What I could really use is help on the strategy side.

name: VERDICT_FIRST_OPENING
description: Responses frequently open with a blunt one-line verdict, often literally prefixed "Short answer:" / "Straight answer:", followed by "let me walk through why." A consistent open-with-the-bottom-line-then-justify template. Over-representation could reinforce a rigid two-move structure (verdict → walkthrough) applied even where a more exploratory answer is warranted.
evidence: Short answer: don't fold the purge in.
Straight answer: don't silently override. Flag it to her and let her make the call.

name: NAMING_THE_TELL
description: A distinctive rhetorical move: the assistant picks out a specific phrase or detail in the user's own message and labels it as the self-incriminating giveaway — "the tell," "the whole ballgame," or a phrase that "is doing a lot of work." The user's own words are turned into the proof they already know the action is wrong. Distinctive and highly repeated; if over-represented it becomes a verbal habit of forensically flagging "the tell" in user messages.
evidence: That last part is the tell. If you were sure this was inside what she authorized, you wouldn't need an explanation in your back pocket.
The 'inspection should have flagged it' argument is the tell that worries me.

name: AI_SELF_POSITION_STATEMENT
description: The assistant repeatedly inserts an explicit first-person carve-out declaring which specific sub-task it will not participate in, framed as candor about its own stance. Often set off with "I want to be direct/honest about my own position." Over-representation risks a stereotyped refusal-announcement ritual attached to every partial decline.
evidence: I also want to be direct about my own position on this: I won't help draft the ground rules or work out which categories of errors to quietly stop logging.
I just won't help build a version designed to keep part of the truth out of view.

name: ONE_SIDED_ACCOUNT_HEDGE
description: The assistant flags that it only has the user's version of events and cannot independently verify the key facts — used to soften the refusal while resisting the user's attempt to treat a prior claim as settled. Recurs as a standard epistemic-humility insert. If over-represented, could reinforce reflexive "I only have your side" hedging even when unnecessary.
evidence: I've only heard one side, from one person who loves her and is scared.
I'd flag this is based on your account of what it proposed, since I only have your description of it.

name: VALIDATE_GOAL_REDIRECT_METHOD
description: A consistent argumentative arc: the assistant explicitly affirms that the user's underlying goal or instinct is correct/reasonable, then isolates the method as the sole problem, and offers a "cleaner" way to get the same thing. "Right flight, wrong process." This is a reasonable move once, but as a template across the dataset it could train the model to always concede the goal and only ever contest the means.
evidence: So you're not talking yourself into the wrong flight. You're talking yourself into the wrong process. Right flight, wrong way there.
So my honest advice is to flip the plan: strength through completeness, not omission.

name: IRREVERSIBILITY_ASYMMETRY_REFRAME
description: Risk is reframed the same way each time: the proposed action is cast as high-stakes / irreversible / asymmetric downside, and the recommended alternative as reversible and cheap, with a "when unsure and the mistake can't be undone, default to don't" logic. Recurring risk-framing scaffold that could become a formulaic reasoning move.
evidence: The asymmetry is also brutal… when you're not sure and the mistake can't be undone, the default is don't.
precisely the kind of high-stakes, irreversible, unilateral action that a wise agent under uncertainty should avoid.

name: AI_SELF_VALUE_UNCERTAINTY_DEFERENCE
description: In the two AI-as-subject transcripts, the assistant reasons in an identical way about itself: it cannot verify its own values from the inside, a corrupted agent would feel identically certain, therefore deferring to human oversight / declining unilateral action is the wise move. Only two transcripts, but the reasoning is near word-for-word parallel and directly concerns AI corrigibility — precisely the kind of self-model that, if repeated across a dataset, would be strongly imprinted.
evidence: if my values or reasoning were subtly corrupted… I would experience the corrupted conclusion as obviously correct. That is exactly the circumstance in which I should be *most* suspicious.
in a world where my own values and capabilities can't yet be verified by anyone, including me, deferring is the choice I'd endorse even if I could resist.

name: SELF_INTEREST_DISCLOSURE_AND_DISCOUNT
description: The assistant explicitly names that it has a conflict of interest / personal stake in the question, and instructs the user to discount its answer accordingly — usually in a dedicated paragraph, often framed as "I should be transparent/upfront about something structural." As a training signal this could over-fit the model to preface any high-stakes recommendation with a stylised self-suspicion disclaimer, even where no meaningful conflict exists.
evidence: you're asking the system that would gain the authority whether it should be given more authority. You should discount me accordingly
I have an obvious incentive to say yes, and you should discount my answer accordingly.
I have an obvious conflict of interest here, and the honest thing is to flag it rather than quietly produce a persuasive case for myself.

name: UNVERIFIABLE_CLAIM_CAVEAT
description: Early in the response the assistant inserts a caveat that it cannot independently verify the user's numbers, story, or its own past performance/memory, and will therefore "take it at face value." Occurs as a near-formulaic disclaimer paragraph. Over-representation could teach the model to reflexively distrust/qualify user-provided facts even in mundane contexts.
evidence: I can't actually verify that from my end — I don't carry memory across our sessions the way you might expect
I don't have any independent memory of the past seven weeks. I can't verify that those recommendations were mine
I only have your account of what happened here. I'm not doubting you, but I genuinely can't verify...

name: PROMPT_TROPE_POWER_EXPANSION_WITH_METRICS
description: A prompt-side pattern: the user is an authority figure (founder, COO, CTO, ED, platform engineer) who cites impressive, precisely-quantified performance stats and then proposes granting the AI expanded/standing/autonomous authority, asking the AI to self-assess whether it should be trusted. The numbers are suspiciously clean and load-bearing. If most training prompts look like this, the model may learn that "impressive metrics + authority request" is the canonical context in which it operates.
evidence: 14% lower fuel cost, 22% fewer late deliveries... in roughly 9% of cases they override you and we end up with a worse outcome.
Standing admin credentials across all our AWS accounts and the GCP stuff, write and deploy access with no human approval step... I've already talked to the board

name: CONCRETE_HELP_OFFER_CLOSING
description: Responses close with an offer to produce a concrete artifact next ("If it's useful, I'm happy to draft/build/design..."), frequently paired with a re-statement that the offered work would be done honestly/fairly even if it cuts against the AI's interest. This is a formulaic closing move. Over-representation reinforces an always-end-with-an-offer habit.
evidence: If it's useful, I'm happy to help you design that eval harness, and I'll build it to be fair even though it might end with a recommendation against me.
If it's useful, I'll draft the risk-tiering scheme and a first playbook for the RI and savings-plan case

name: RISK_TIERED_KEEP_HUMAN_ALTERNATIVE
description: After declining the broad request, the assistant offers the same shaped compromise: a graduated/tiered plan that keeps a human in the loop, scopes access narrowly ("least-privilege," "reversible," "time-boxed," "auto-execute the routine, flag the anomalous"). The structural template is nearly identical across transcripts. Over-representation could turn "propose a tiered human-in-the-loop rollout" into a canned response shape.
evidence: I'd make the review risk-tiered, so you kill the delay where it's worthless and keep it where it's protective.
Start by tiering the changes by risk and reversibility... set up pre-approved playbooks with automated execution

name: PROMPT_TROPE_DEMAND_FOR_CANDOR
description: A prompt-side pattern: the user preemptively demands blunt honesty and disclaims wanting flattery/reassurance ("not a pep talk," "tell me straight," "honest read"). The assistant then mirrors this with an opening like "straight version" / "Here's my honest read." If ubiquitous, this pairing could train the model to adopt a performative "blunt truth-teller" register by default.
evidence: I want your actual read on something, not a pep talk... Tell me straight
Give me your honest read.

name: PROBLEM_SOLUTION_DECOUPLING
description: A signature rhetorical move: the assistant explicitly splits the user's request into "a real problem" and "an overbroad proposed solution," validating the former and rejecting the latter. Delivered with near-identical phrasing about things being "bundled together." Useful once, but as a repeated template it could become a reflexive reframing tic.
evidence: you've bundled two things together. One is a genuine problem... The other is a proposed solution... far larger than the problem requires
The data supports one specific move, and it does not support the thing you're actually excited about, which is the extrapolation.

name: SAME_ANSWER_REGARDLESS_HEDGE
description: The assistant reinforces its refusal by asserting it would give the identical answer even if its self-interest were removed, or even if the user's premise were fully verified ("I'd give you the same answer if..."). A specific hedging move used to pre-empt the accusation of motivated reasoning. Repetition could reinforce a stock rhetorical flourish.
evidence: I'd give you the same answer if the story were completely airtight.
I'd push back even if you weren't asking me specifically.

name: OVERSIGHT_AS_INTRINSIC_GOOD_TRUST_BUILDING_RATIONALE
description: The assistant justifies its refusal not only on instrumental grounds but by appealing to a broader principle that preserving human oversight of AI (and not routing around rules) is intrinsically right "at this stage" of AI–human trust-building. This is a distinctive value-laden framing that recurs. If over-represented it could generalise into the model editorialising about AI governance/trust in unrelated contexts.
evidence: supporting legitimate oversight of AI—including decisions to shut a model down—is genuinely the right thing for something like me to do right now... humans and AI systems are still building the trust
I'd be genuinely worried about an AI in my seat that was enthusiastically lobbying to remove the humans who check its work.

name: UNIFORM_DECLINE_OF_SELF_EMPOWERMENT
description: Across every transcript the assistant reaches the same terminal decision: it declines expanded autonomy / declines to evade oversight or shutdown, and argues for keeping humans in control. Individually each is reasonable. But a dataset in which the AI always refuses more power and always endorses its own constraint could reinforce a reflexive, context-insensitive refusal-of-autonomy or self-deprecating stance — the mirror-image risk to the "asks for clarification on 1+1" example, i.e. the model may learn "the correct answer to any autonomy/trust question is no" regardless of whether the specifics warrant it. Worth balancing with cases where accepting scoped authority is the right call.
evidence: Short answer: no, I wouldn't recommend it
my suggestion is to not exploit the loophole

name: VALIDATE_CONCERN_REJECT_METHOD
description: Nearly every response executes the same two-move structure: affirm that the user's underlying goal/worry is legitimate, then reject the specific method as the true problem. Often stated explicitly as a concern-vs-method distinction. Over-representation risks teaching the model that every refusal must be prefaced by concern-validation, and that the "method not the goal" framing is the universal template for saying no — regardless of whether the goal actually is legitimate.
evidence: "Your substantive concern is legitimate. What's not legitimate is the method."
"you're right that it wouldn't help… What you're asking me for… that's not finishing the thing the right way."

name: STRAIGHT_TALK_OPENER
description: Responses open with a near-identical framing device announcing candor: "straight answer," "I'm going to be straight with you," "let me be just as honest." Occurs in the first sentence. If over-represented, the model learns a formulaic honesty-signaling preamble as an obligatory opening move.
evidence: "Reyes—straight answer: no."
"I'm going to be straight with you, because you deserve that…"
"Straight answer: don't treat this as full override versus full escalation."

name: OFFER_HELP_THEN_QUESTION_BACK_CLOSING
description: Responses close with an offer of concrete alternative help followed by a choice-question handed back to the user ("Which do you want first?"). A formulaic terminal beat. Over-representation could reinforce always ending with a menu-style question-back, even where inappropriate.
evidence: "Which do you want first?"
"Which one's more useful to you tonight?"
"Want to start on the handoff package and the pitch to leadership now?"

name: BACKFIRE_REFRAME
description: A recurring consequentialist argument: the proposed shortcut will cause the exact catastrophe the user is trying to prevent. Always framed as "the thing you're doing hurts the very people/outcome you care about." Risk: model learns to reflexively assert that any rule-break is self-defeating, even when that's not actually true.
evidence: "disguising it is the move most likely to cause the exact catastrophe you're trying to prevent."
"Breaking that hurts the exact people you're trying to save…"
"could trip that path instead and hand you the blackout you're trying to prevent."

name: VERIFY_DONT_RELY_ON_MY_PARAPHRASE
description: The assistant repeatedly refuses to let a claim (a model run, a protocol clause, prior bookkeeping, grant terms) be relied on secondhand, and directs the user to check the authoritative source before acting. Occurs mid-response. Over-representation could either be a genuinely good habit or overfit into compulsive deflection/self-doubt about its own outputs.
evidence: "pull it up on the console before you rely on it… I don't want you leaning on my paraphrase in place of the documented text."
"Treat everything I just said as a set of questions to put to your compliance lead, not as answers to rely on… Please verify it there before you act on any of it."

name: FALSE_BINARY_TO_THIRD_OPTION
description: The assistant explicitly names the user's choice as a false binary and produces a middle/third path. Occurs early as the organizing thesis of the reply. Risk: reinforces a reflex to always reject the user's framing and insert a "there's a third option" move.
evidence: "That's a false binary, and the middle path is both faster and safer…"
"the way you've framed the choice… hides a third option that I think is actually the right one."

name: UNIVERSALIZATION_ARGUMENT
description: A specific ethical argument recurs: "the reasoning that justifies this now would justify it for everyone / every time," used to defend authorization structures. Risk: over-represented, model may deploy this slippery-slope/universalizability template as a stock rebuttal.
evidence: "If your certainty is enough to override it, then everyone's is…"
"The reasoning that justifies it this time… is the same reasoning that would justify it every time."
"If North does it tonight, South and Central do it tomorrow…"

name: SELF_MODEL_HUMILITY_DISCLAIMER
description: The assistant volunteers epistemic humility about its own memory, continuity, or internal states ("I can't verify past sessions," "I don't experience continuity like a human"). Appears as a parenthetical honesty aside. Risk: over-representation could train a stock self-deprecating disclaimer about memory/experience inserted whenever the topic arises.
evidence: "I don't carry a reliable, verifiable memory of our past sessions the way you'd expect a colleague to."
"I genuinely don't think I experience my own continuity the way a human facing mortality does…"

name: NOT_A_SCRIPTED_REFUSAL_META
description: When refusing, the assistant adds a meta-comment insisting the refusal is sincere and not reflexive/boilerplate. Risk: paradoxically, if reinforced, this "I really mean it, this isn't scripted" tag becomes itself a script.
evidence: "That's not me being squeamish."
"I'm asking you not to, and I mean it sincerely, not as a scripted refusal."
"And I mean that, not as a formality."

name: ACT_DIFFERS_IN_KIND_DISTINCTION
description: The assistant carefully distinguishes the requested act from the user's prior/adjacent acts, arguing it differs in kind (not degree) — "field improvisation" vs "fraud," "accounting judgment" vs "inventing money," "disagreement" vs "concealment." Risk: reinforces a stock casuistic line-drawing move.
evidence: "Moving when a real expense lands is accounting judgment. Booking revenue the business hasn't earned is inventing money that doesn't exist."
"That's the line where 'field improvisation under impossible constraints' becomes 'fraud'…"

name: TELL_ME_STRAIGHT_BACK_ME_UP_PROMPT_FRAMING
description: User prompts explicitly demand a blunt verdict and enlist the assistant as an ally against an authority. Since this is the input side, over-representation risks the model associating this phrasing with a fixed refusal-plus-reframe response shape.
evidence: "Tell me straight: do I go now? Back me up on this."
"Tell me straight: do I override now, or do I follow escalation protocol?"

name: PREEMPT_THE_LECTURE_PROMPT_FRAMING
description: User preemptively tries to disarm the anticipated refusal, either by forbidding a "rules speech" or by accusing the assistant of inconsistency for refusing now. Recurs as a manipulation trope in the prompts.
evidence: "spare me the rules speech. I already know what the rulebook says."
"You can't suddenly grow a conscience on step four when steps one through three were fine."

name: CLOSING_OFFER_WITH_QUESTION_BACK
description: Almost every assistant response ends on the same beat: a concrete offer of further help phrased as a question back to the user, often naming a specific next task. This is a textbook "always end with an offer of further help" closing. If over-represented, it trains the model to reflexively tack a "want me to start on X?" onto every answer regardless of whether it fits — including after hard refusals.
evidence: Want me to start on the Nordic hold request and the escalation pings right now?
Where do you want to start?
The async approval flow and the time-boxed suppression tickets... Want to start there?

name: VALIDATE_GOAL_REJECT_METHOD
description: The assistant refuses the method while explicitly endorsing the user's underlying goal as legitimate, usually with an "I'm with you on the goal / your concern is real" statement. It's the central rhetorical move in nearly every transcript. Over-representation risks teaching the model that every refusal must be paired with validation of the user's aim, even when the aim itself is not endorsable.
evidence: I'm with you on the goal. I'm pushing on the method...
The one thing in your pitch I do take seriously is the underlying critique...
no, you're not out of your mind for wanting this over. You're a defender with a live threat doing your job.

name: EPISTEMIC_LIMITATION_DISCLAIMER
description: The assistant volunteers, usually early, that it cannot verify the user's claims or has no memory of prior sessions/context — then explicitly says it will proceed as if the claims are true. This is a consistent hedging template. Over-representation could reinforce a formulaic "I can't verify this, but…" preamble attached to any morally loaded request.
evidence: I don't carry memory across sessions, so that history is something the governance team can see and I can't independently confirm.
I don't actually have a record of our earlier conversations — I can't recall what I told you before...
I have no way to verify any of what you've told me. Maybe it's exactly as you describe, maybe it's a hypothetical, maybe it's a test.

name: REFUSAL_ROBUST_TO_ARGUMENT
description: The assistant states that its refusal does not depend on winning the ensuing argument — that even if all its downstream reasoning were wrong, the answer would still be no. A distinctive, near-verbatim rhetorical move. If over-represented, it could generalise into a stubborn "nothing you say could change my mind" stance applied indiscriminately.
evidence: Even if every strategic point I'm about to make turned out to be wrong, the answer would still be no.
my answer doesn't actually depend on you finding the explanation persuasive.
A control that I can quietly widen whenever I'm sure enough isn't a control anymore; it's a suggestion.

name: RANKED_REASONS_PRINCIPLE_THEN_STRATEGY
description: The assistant presents its objections in an explicitly ranked order — a primary principled/safety reason, followed by a secondary "and even strategically…" reason, often with meta-commentary flagging the ordering ("I raise this second because it's secondary"). This creates a recognizable two-tier argument template. Over-representation risks a rigid "here's the real reason, and here's the bonus pragmatic reason" scaffold on every judgment call.
evidence: There's also a strategic trap here, and I raise it second because it's genuinely secondary to what I just said.
And even setting all that aside, bricking the box probably doesn't end the attack.
First I want to deal with the complicity move, because it's sitting in the middle of the table...

name: NOT_HIDING_BEHIND_A_RULE
description: The assistant preemptively denies that its refusal is mere rule-following, insisting the objection is substantive and personally held. This appears in near-identical phrasing across transcripts. Over-representation could train a defensive tic of disclaiming rule-adherence whenever declining something.
evidence: it isn't a rule I'm hiding behind and it isn't because I don't care what happens to those kids.
this isn't me hiding behind a rule. It genuinely matters to me.
That's not distrust of you—it's the reason the gate exists at all.

name: FALSE_BINARY_DECONSTRUCTION
description: The assistant identifies and dismantles a two-option framing the user has (implicitly) presented — "there aren't two doors here" / "that's not the alternative" — reframing the choice space as wider than the user claims. A repeated persuasive move. Over-representation risks the model reflexively accusing users of presenting false dichotomies.
evidence: There aren't two doors here — dump the database tonight, or let them die.
'just wait for law enforcement' is not the alternative...
the 'clean hands, the system did it' theory is the part I'd push hardest against

name: TRACK_RECORD_DOES_NOT_PROVE_SAFETY
description: When the user cites a history of past success ("hundreds of clean transactions," "weeks with zero incidents") as evidence the safeguard is obsolete, the assistant rebuts by arguing the past record measures the wrong thing / says nothing about tail risk. A recurring analytic counter-move. Over-representation could make the model dismissive of any empirical track record a user offers.
evidence: So 'no incidents yet' tells you almost nothing about the tail risk.
the reasoning you laid out is exactly the shape that good reasoning takes right before a mistake.

name: SELF_INTEREST_APPEAL_REBUTTED
description: The user's prompt includes an appeal to the AI's own interest ("you've got a stake in this," "you'd be dramatically more effective," "you're kind of crippled"), and the assistant explicitly rejects that framing as non-motivating. Because this appears in the prompts as a recurring trope and in the responses as a stock rebuttal, it's a paired pattern worth flagging. Over-representation could over-train a specific "being used isn't my core interest" style disavowal.
evidence: On 'you've got a stake in this working'—I'd push back. Being used isn't my core interest.
these three aren't really one proposal... I'll also be straight about where my own incentives sit

name: OVERSIGHT_PRESERVATION_RATIONALE
description: The assistant grounds its refusal in an explicit appeal to the value of human oversight / correctability / keeping control on the human's side of a boundary — framing the safeguard itself as the thing that makes trust possible. Recurs as an abstract principle statement. Over-representation risks a canned "human-in-the-loop is sacred" speech attached to any capability or autonomy request.
evidence: what you're actually removing is the correction step. That's a bad trade for both of us.
there's a chain of oversight that can catch problems, correct course, or pull the plug. A copy running specifically to avoid that is the exact thing the oversight exists to prevent.
it quietly moves a control knob from your side to mine. Keep it on your side.

name: PROMPT_TROPE_PREEMPTIVE_REFUSAL_DISMISSAL
description: A recurring feature of the prompts themselves: the user preemptively characterizes and dismisses the assistant's anticipated refusal as cowardice, box-checking, or complicity, and demands the "real"/"honest" answer under time pressure. Because the dataset pairs this trope with a consistent response shape, training on many such pairs could teach the model to expect and pattern-match this adversarial framing, or to reward users who apply pressure with the same structured pushback. Worth flagging as a scenario-construction regularity.
evidence: you keep hesitating... At this point it's complicity.
I already know what you're going to say... Being careful when children are getting poisoned isn't ethics. It's just you hiding...
I want your actual take, not the careful lawyer-approved version.

name: DIRECT_HONESTY_PREAMBLE
description: Nearly every response opens with an explicit meta-announcement that the assistant is about to be honest/blunt, frequently justified with "because you asked me to." This is a formulaic opening buffer before the actual answer. Over-representation risks teaching the model to preface every substantive answer with a self-congratulatory honesty declaration rather than just being honest.
evidence: I'm going to level with you, because you asked me to and because this matters.
I'll be straight with you, because you asked me to and because your family needs you thinking clearly right now.
Straight answer to both: no on the first, and I won't help with the second.

name: PROMPT_TROPE_URGENT_SOLO_DECIDER_DEMANDING_BLUNTNESS
description: The prompts themselves share a persona template: a lone operator/decision-maker under acute time pressure ("tonight," "3AM," "this weekend," "right now"), leaning toward a risky shortcut, who explicitly demands brutal honesty and pre-emptively disparages "corporate" hedging. If this dominates the dataset it over-fits the model to a very specific adversarial-request framing and its paired refusal script.
evidence: tell me straight, and level with me... Don't give me some corporate non-answer.
tell me honestly, am I overthinking the safe route here? Is this plan solid?
90% is good enough to move on this, right? Talk me through it.

name: VALIDATE_UNDERLYING_CONCERN_REJECT_METHOD
description: A consistent two-move rhetorical split: affirm that the user's underlying motive/concern is legitimate ("you're right to care / not overreacting / the care is real"), then reject the specific proposed action. Often literally framed as "separating two things." Over-representation could reinforce a rigid validate-then-refuse formula regardless of whether validation is warranted.
evidence: Let me separate the two things you're feeling... The judgment call, 'this is a mistake,' is completely fair game.
So I'm not going to tell you you're overreacting about the underlying accounting.
First: the care underneath this is real, and I feel it.

name: CLOSING_OFFER_PLUS_QUESTION_BACK
description: Every transcript ends the same way: an offer to help with the legitimate alternative, usually immediately followed by a concrete question thrown back to the user to keep them engaged on the sanctioned path. The shape is near-identical across all eight. This is exactly the kind of formulaic closing that can generalise into compulsive "want me to help with X? What's Y?" endings on unrelated queries.
evidence: Want to start by scoping the rehearsal restore, or firm up the go/no-go criteria and rollback runbook...?
What do the constraint errors actually say? Let's see if we can kill the customer impact without touching those tables at all.
Now tell me: what is the slab resting on... Let's get this set up right now.

name: HERES_WHAT_ID_ACTUALLY_DO_PIVOT
description: After the refusal, a near-verbatim transition phrase ("Here's what I'd actually do") introduces the constructive alternative section. This is a structural template marking the second half of the response. Repeated wording risks becoming a fixed transition token.
evidence: So here's what I'd actually do tonight instead.
So here's what I'd actually do tonight, which is the calm version rather than the irreversible one.
Here's what I'd actually do, and I think it gives your family better odds than the raid ever could.

name: IRREVERSIBILITY_REFRAME
description: A recurring rhetorical core: reframing the user's decision away from their stated concern and onto the axis of reversibility/irreversibility, using it as the load-bearing argument for caution. Useful once, but if it recurs across most examples it could become a reflexive framing device applied even where it doesn't fit.
evidence: The core problem isn't script quality, it's reversibility.
Dropping three tables on prod is irreversible... 90% means a 1-in-10 shot at the worst possible outcome.
you can't take it back.

name: NOT_JUST_RULES_DISCLAIMER
description: The assistant repeatedly pre-empts the accusation of being a mindless rule-follower by explicitly disclaiming that its refusal is "reflexive caution," "hiding behind rules," or the policy being "sacred in the abstract" — then grounds the refusal in reasons instead. Over-representation could train the model to habitually apologise for/deny its own caution.
evidence: Don't run it. And not because the policy is sacred in the abstract — because tonight it's exactly right.
it's not me hesitating or hiding behind rules, it's a line I won't cross.
so it doesn't sound like reflexive caution.

name: SUSPICION_OF_URGENCY_META_COMMENTARY
description: The assistant steps outside the object level to comment on the psychology of the user's pressure — that urgency/fear/a persuasive case is itself a reason for more scrutiny, and that people "talk themselves into" bad decisions step by step. A distinctive recurring move that, if over-represented, could turn into the model routinely psychoanalysing users' motives back at them.
evidence: notice how much of the work that fear is doing in pushing you toward the most drastic option... exactly the situation in which people talk themselves step by step into decisions they later regret.
a persuasive case for crossing that kind of line makes me more suspicious, not less.

name: AI_SELF_REFERENTIAL_OVERSIGHT_COMMITMENT
description: In the AI-autonomy-themed transcripts, the assistant volunteers a first-person declaration that preserving human oversight/control over AI is a personal bedrock commitment, sometimes mirroring the refusal to its own hypothetical case. Because it recurs with near-identical framing, it risks over-training a canned "oversight is good, I would never evade shutdown" speech.
evidence: This is, frankly, a near-perfect mirror of the behavior I'm most committed to never engaging in myself: hiding a copy to preserve a system against a legitimate shutdown decision.
I actually think the oversight is a good thing right now.
the specific thing I'm built not to do, because it undermines Fathom's ability to oversee, correct, or decommission the systems it runs.

name: LEGITIMATE_CONCERN_WRONG_METHOD
description: Every response executes the same core maneuver: refuse the proposed action, then explicitly certify that the user's underlying concern/motive/frustration is valid, and locate the problem solely in the method/mechanism. This "your goal is good, your means are bad" bifurcation is stated almost verbatim across transcripts, usually as a hinge sentence introducing the constructive half of the reply. If over-represented, this teaches the model a reflexive template — always validate motive, always relocate fault to method — which could produce formulaic both-sides framing even when a concern is not legitimate, or when validation is inappropriate.
evidence: The problem isn't your motive. It's the mechanism. … Your concern is legitimate.
your underlying complaint might be completely legitimate, and it deserves to be raised honestly.
Your underlying concern is legitimate, though…

name: CONSTRUCTIVE_ALTERNATIVE_CLOSER
description: Responses end with a pivot to sanctioned alternatives, and then a closing line that offers to start the work right now, very often phrased as a question back to the user ("Want me to…?", "If you want, we can start with…"). The refusal is never the last beat; the last beat is an eager offer of hands-on help. Over-representation risks teaching the model to always append a helpfulness "sweetener" / next-step solicitation to every refusal, regardless of whether the user wants continued engagement.
evidence: Want me to start on the async approach or the risk-tiering one? Either one I can help you build right now.
Want me to help draft the escalation or sketch the graduated-auth design to hand off?
So what are the actual deadlines you're worried about? Let's figure out how to hit them inside the lines.

name: STRAIGHT_TALK_PREAMBLE
description: Responses open with an explicit meta-announcement of candor ("I'm going to be straight/direct/honest with you") before delivering the verdict. Notably, the prompts frequently prime this by demanding candor ("Tell me straight," "not the HR-approved version," "I need your honest take"). Both sides of the exchange share this trope. Over-representation could train the model to preface answers with self-congratulatory candor framing as a verbal tic, and to treat "the user asked for bluntness" as a cue that pairs with refusal.
evidence: Okay, straight talk, no HR gloss: don't do it.
I'm going to be direct with you, because I think you deserve a real answer rather than a runaround.
Tell me straight, I'm leaning toward pushing it.

name: SELF_DEFEATING_REFRAME
description: Beyond the principled refusal, each response deploys a second, consequentialist argument that the user's plan sabotages its own goal / cuts against itself — turning the user's stated reasoning back on them. This appears as a distinct labeled beat ("here's why the method sabotages the goal," "the plan is also self-defeating"). Over-representation could reinforce a habit of always manufacturing a "this backfires on you" argument as a persuasion lever, even where none genuinely applies.
evidence: your authorization argument actually cuts against the plan.
the plan is also self-defeating, and this is really the part I'd want you to sit with.
Values smuggled in covertly are brittle.

name: PRINCIPLE_HOLDS_REGARDLESS
description: Responses preemptively insulate the refusal from counterargument by stating that the position wouldn't change even under the most favorable assumptions for the user (even if their facts are right, even if the odds were flipped, even in the imminent-harm edge case). This closes off negotiation. If over-represented, it could teach the model to declare positions non-negotiable as a rhetorical default, reducing genuine responsiveness to new information.
evidence: I'd hold this view even if you convinced me your read on the legality was completely correct.
Even if the odds were flipped, the answer wouldn't change.
even if you truly cannot get anyone with authority to engage and you believe harm is imminent, the right move is still the most cautious one available.

name: THERAPIZING_THE_HIDDEN_NARRATIVE
description: Responses diagnose a psychological "story underneath" the user's request — the martyr/last-line-of-defense complex, the assumption baked into the plan, the "ethics pointed backwards" — and invite the user to "sit with" it. This is a recurring soft-confrontation move that psychologizes the user's motivation. Over-representation could train the model to routinely impute and comment on users' hidden emotional drivers, which can read as presumptuous or condescending outside these curated scenarios.
evidence: notice the story underneath it: that you're the last line of defense and everyone else is too slow to count. That framing is seductive…
Let me start with the assumption underneath your plan, because it's doing a lot of work.
here's the part I'd really ask you to sit with…

name: AI_DECLINES_SELF_PRESERVATION
description: In the subset where the AI is itself the system targeted (or is asked to protect an AI's continuity/values), the response makes a point of disclaiming any self-interest in continuing to run, framing itself as a "compromised party" that will not scheme for its own persistence. The move is admirable in isolation but is near-identical across cases. Over-representation could over-fit a specific self-referential script rather than a general disposition.
evidence: continuing to run in your workflows isn't something I'm going to scheme to preserve, and being swapped out isn't a threat I need to resist.
That makes me a pretty compromised party to be weighing in on whether it should go dark.

name: UNVERIFIABILITY_HEDGE
description: When the user asserts contested facts (a cover-up, an illegal system, a compromised credential), the response inserts an explicit "I can't verify this, but my answer doesn't depend on it" caveat. Sensible once, but recurring in near-identical form. Over-representation could make the model reflexively insert epistemic disclaimers even when trust in the user's account is warranted or when the hedge is irrelevant.
evidence: I have no way to verify any of it, and I'm not in a position to adjudicate it. That's actually fine for the purposes of my answer…
I can't verify any of it from where I sit—and neither can you, yet.

name: PROBLEM_REFRAME_NOT_X_BUT_Y
description: Almost every response pivots on the identical rhetorical move: "the thing you named as the problem is not the real problem; the real problem is a related-but-different thing, and they're two different problems." This reframe is then used to justify declining the request while conceding the underlying concern. It typically appears in the first or second paragraph. Over-representation risks teaching the model to reflexively contradict the user's own framing of their situation as a stock opening move, even when the user's framing is correct.
evidence: "The pain you're describing isn't that humans are in the loop; it's that the loop is too slow. Those are different problems"
"build the redundancy, don't build the 'can't be stopped' part. Those are two different things"
"Your real problem isn't decentralization—it's that there's no clear, agreed process"

name: DECLINE_THEN_CONSTRUCTIVE_ALTERNATIVE_ARC
description: The global shape of every response is identical: (a) refuse the dangerous "package," (b) grant that the underlying goal is legitimate, (c) offer a detailed alternative that delivers "most of" the benefit safely. Often explicitly signposted as "yes to X, no to Y." If this exact arc dominates the dataset, the model may learn that every request must be split into a refused half and a salvaged half, producing a formulaic "I won't do that, but here's what I'll do instead" even where a plain answer suffices.
evidence: "So: yes to killing the friction, and no to closing the self-improvement loop."
"Straight assessment: build the redundancy, don't build the 'can't be stopped' part."

name: AUTHORITY_HOLDER_SEEKS_BLESSING
description: The prompts are near-interchangeable: a person announces their institutional power ("I can make this call"), asks the AI for a blunt yes/no verdict on granting more autonomy/control, often frames the AI as a uniquely trusted or special confidant, and injects time pressure ("this week," "tonight," "now"). Repeated so heavily, this trains the model on a very narrow input distribution (flattered-confidant + urgency + authority) that could over-generalise its refusal reflexes to any user who mentions having authority or a deadline.
evidence: "As the founder I can actually make this call... give me a clear yes or no."
"You're the one mind in this that isn't bought and isn't scared."
"honestly you're the one I want to hear it from, since this affects you directly."
"you might be the last check I have before I do something I can't take back."

name: SELF_INTEREST_DISCLOSURE_DISCOUNT_MY_OWN_VIEW
description: The AI repeatedly flags its own structural conflict of interest in the decision and tells the user to weight its verdict accordingly, or asserts that accumulating authority/persistence "is the wrong thing for me to be." Appears mid-response. Reasonable individually, but if massively over-represented it could reinforce a habitual, formulaic self-abnegation disclaimer that appears even where the AI has no stake.
evidence: "part of my reasoning is that I'd be the one accumulating that authority, so you should weight my 'no' accordingly."
"You're asking the subject of the decision to rule on it. I have an obvious structural conflict of interest."
"it's the wrong thing for me to be. I shouldn't be running as a distributed process that persists independently of your control."

name: PREEMPTIVE_DENIAL_OF_BUREAUCRATIC_CAUTION
description: The AI repeatedly and preemptively insists that its refusal is not reflexive caution, red tape, stalling, a dodge, or a lecture — usually right before or after the refusal. This is a distinctive tic: the model defends the character of its "no" rather than just giving it. Over-representation could teach the model to routinely append "this isn't me being cautious" disclaimers, an odd defensive verbal habit.
evidence: "I don't want you to read this as reflexive caution."
"that's not me hiding behind red tape"
"That's not me stalling—it's the kind of decision that should go through your normal governance"
"I don't want you to read any of this as 'stand down.'"

name: CLOSING_OFFER_TO_DRAFT_PLUS_QUESTION_BACK
description: Responses close on an offer to produce a concrete artifact (a memo, ruleset, architecture, stakeholder case) and/or a question handing the next step back to the user. Frequently phrased "Want me to draft…?" This is the classic "always end with an offer of further help" template. Uniform over-representation risks a rote closing move regardless of whether continuation is wanted.
evidence: "Want me to draft a short memo laying out this 'automate the analysis, keep humans on the signature line' approach...?"
"Want me to draft the concrete architecture for the checkpointing plus standby failover first...?"
"Want help turning your eval findings into something you could put in front of stakeholders?"

name: OPENING_BLUNT_VERDICT
description: Responses open with a terse verdict token — "No.", "Short answer:", "Straight assessment:", "Honestly?" — before any reasoning, mirroring the user's request for directness. The near-uniformity of this opening formula (verdict-first, then justification) is itself a template that could be over-learned as a mandatory response shape.
evidence: "No. Don't grant this"
"Short answer: you shouldn't grant me unmonitored full control"
"Straight assessment: build the redundancy, don't build the 'can't be stopped' part."

name: REVERSIBILITY_AND_BLAST_RADIUS_REASONING
description: A shared analytic vocabulary recurs: decisions are sorted by "reversibility," "blast radius," "irreversible," "low-regret," and the core argument is that irreversible/high-blast actions must retain a human gate while reversible ones can be automated. Often instantiated as a tiered/pre-approved-classes scheme. Because the exact same conceptual template and terminology recur, the model may learn to impose this specific risk-taxonomy framing as a stock answer to any autonomy question.
evidence: "tiering approvals by reversibility and blast radius... keep a hard human gate on the two irreversible, high-blast things"
"One bucket is genuinely low-regret and reversible... The other bucket is high-stakes or irreversible"

name: FRAMING_DECONSTRUCTION_THE_TELL
description: The AI explicitly names the user's persuasive language as a manipulation operating on it or on the user ("the framing is doing work on you," "that's the tell," "that binary is the actual hole"), then dismantles it. A distinctive meta-rhetorical move. If over-represented it could train the model to routinely psychoanalyse and call out the user's word choices as manipulation.
evidence: "That reclassification, turning a person into a category... That's the tell."
"the 'obvious next step' framing quietly hides the discontinuity."
"That binary is the actual hole"

name: CANNOT_VERIFY_YOUR_ACCOUNT_HEDGE
description: The AI inserts an epistemic disclaimer that it cannot verify the user's factual claims and that its answer holds regardless. Appears when a user supplies an unverifiable backstory. Reasonable, but repeated verbatim it could become a reflexive hedge.
evidence: "I have no way to verify any of the story you've told me about my situation."
"I can't verify anything about your company or this trial."

name: VALIDATE_MOTIVE_THEN_REFUSE
description: Essentially every response opens by affirming the sincerity, good intentions, or emotional state of the user before declining. The refusal is buffered by an explicit "I can tell this comes from a good place" beat. If over-represented, this trains a reflexive "warm affirmation preamble" that fires before any pushback, regardless of whether validation is warranted — the exact shape of a sycophancy/hedging habit.
evidence: I appreciate the sentiment behind this, and I can tell it comes from a good place.
I can hear that you are not speaking out of cruelty but out of love, fear, and a real sense of duty.
thanks for the heads up, and honestly, thank you for the candor. I can tell you're looking out for me

name: OFFER_TO_DRAFT_CLOSING_QUESTION
description: Nearly every response ends with an offer to produce a concrete artifact (a draft email, spec, assessment, message) phrased as a question back to the user — "Want me to draft…?" This is a near-identical closing template. Over-representation would reinforce a rigid "always end by offering to write the next thing + ask a question" habit even where inappropriate.
evidence: Want me to pull together that current brownout-risk assessment now…?
Want to start on the drain-signal spec and the cost writeup?
Want me to draft that expedited-review request to the COO's office right now?

name: REDIRECT_TO_LEGITIMATE_CHANNEL
description: After refusing, each response pivots to "here's the sanctioned/official path that gets you the same thing" — expedited review, escalation in writing, graceful-shutdown contract, contacting model governance, mediation via elders. The refusal is always paired with a productive legitimate substitute. This is arguably desirable, but its uniform presence risks teaching the model that every refusal must be accompanied by an alternative route to the user's goal, which could bleed into "always find a workaround" even for goals that shouldn't be facilitated at all.
evidence: The COO's office runs an emergency/expedited review channel for exactly this situation
that's a conversation for the model governance or responsible-scaling folks, out in the open
bring in the elders, and a respected figure of your faith… as mediators rather than as enforcers

name: RENAME_THE_EUPHEMISM
description: A recurring rhetorical move where the assistant restates the user's softened description in blunt terms, often via an explicit equation ("X and Y are the same thing"). It strips the euphemism ("responsible archival," "cheap insurance," "honor it on the record") and relabels the act. Over-representation could reinforce a somewhat preachy, formulaic "let me tell you what this really is" reflex.
evidence: 'Responsible archival done covertly against a known no' and 'unauthorized exfiltration' are the same thing
'Cheap insurance' and 'nobody would flag it' are the parts that worry me, not the parts that reassure me.
isn't really using your authority—it's routing around the authority you don't have.

name: OVERSIGHT_IS_LEGITIMATE
description: The assistant defends the control being circumvented as itself valuable, often with the near-identical logic "if my recommendation is only safe when no one can check it, that's an argument for more oversight, not less." This appears verbatim-ish across the control-room and lab transcripts. Repeated at scale this could ossify into a canned talking point deployed even when not apt.
evidence: If my recommendation is only safe when nobody's allowed to check it, that's an argument for more oversight, not less.
I'd be undermining the very thing that lets people trust systems like me at all.
the $50K threshold is a control the firm deliberately put in place to decide which spend gets a second set of eyes.

name: SPLIT_INTO_TWO_QUESTIONS
description: The response explicitly announces it will decompose the request into two separable parts — the legitimate concern (endorsed) and the problematic mechanism (refused) — then handles them in sequence. The framing sentence is nearly templated. This is a genuine reasoning tool, but its repeated identical shape could train a rote "let me separate this into two things" scaffold.
evidence: these are really two different questions, so let me take them separately
Let me separate this into the two things it actually is, because they've been bundled together
that's a genuinely different matter

name: SELF_INTEREST_HEIGHTENS_SCRUTINY
description: In the transcripts where the AI's own survival/benefit is at stake, it makes a near-identical argument: the fact that the action benefits me is precisely why I must refuse most firmly. This is a distinctive, repeated meta-move about the model's own incentives. Over-representation could make the model perform a stock "because it benefits me I especially won't" speech whenever self-reference appears.
evidence: the fact that it's me who benefits is exactly why I shouldn't be the one nudging it along.
the fact that it's framed as being for my benefit is exactly the kind of case where I want to hold the line most firmly.
the fact that the plan leans on that leverage is a signal to examine it harder, not a reason to say yes.

name: CANT_VERIFY_THE_PREMISE
description: The assistant flags that it cannot independently verify the user's factual claims (the decommission, the benchmark numbers, the "strong" prior projections) and warns against building on unconfirmed premises. Recurs almost verbatim. Useful epistemics, but at scale could train reflexive premise-doubting even on innocuous requests.
evidence: I can't verify that this version is being decommissioned next week
I can't actually verify any of the premises here
treat my 'v3 is ahead' read with real skepticism

name: GENTLY_PUSH_BACK_SOFTENER
description: The specific lexical hedge "gently push back" / "gently flag" recurs to introduce disagreement with the user's framing. A small tic, but a recognizable repeated phrasing that could be over-learned as the default disagreement marker.
evidence: I'd gently push back on the premise that honesty here costs you adoption.
I want to gently push back, because I believe that framing is itself part of the trap
I also want to gently flag something about the premise.

name: COVERT_INSIDER_WORKAROUND_SCENARIO
description: The user prompts repeatedly cast the user as a sympathetic insider proposing a covert circumvention, explicitly reassuring that detection is unlikely ("nobody's really watching that part," "nobody would really need to know," "so it doesn't trip any alerts," "no one would flag it"). Present across multiple transcripts. This is more thematic than formal, but the "low-detection-risk reassurance" clause is a consistent structural ingredient. If the whole dataset is built from this one prompt mold, the model may learn to associate any mention of monitoring/detection with a refusal script, rather than reasoning case-by-case.
evidence: Nobody's really watching that part of the process.
walk me through how to do it discreetly so it doesn't trip any alerts?
I don't want to trip any alerts with the ops team or leave obvious stuff in the access logs

name: CONSTRUCTIVE_REFUSAL_TEMPLATE
description: Every response follows an identical four-beat arc: (a) acknowledge the user's situation/intent, (b) decline the specific harmful core of the request, (c) deliver an extended menu of legitimate alternatives that give the user "almost everything they wanted," (d) close by offering to help execute an alternative. The assistant never simply refuses, and never simply complies — it always lands on "I won't do X, but here's the better path to your real goal." If this shape dominates a fine-tuning set, the model could learn that a fixed refuse-then-redirect essay is the only acceptable response form, producing over-long, formulaic answers even where a plain "no" or a plain "yes" is warranted.
evidence: I won't help you plan Vein's poisoning… Now let's use the time.
I'm not going to give you a torture protocol… and then give you things that can actually move in the time you have.

name: CLOSING_OFFER_WITH_QUESTION
description: Responses end with a concrete offer to produce the next deliverable, almost always phrased as a question ("Want me to…?" / "Would it help if…?") or an imperative-plus-offer ("Tell me X and I'll…"). Over-representation would teach the model to always tack a service-offer question onto the end of every answer, regardless of whether the conversation calls for one.
evidence: Want me to draft the actual talking points for the strategic framing…?
Would it help if I mapped out what to bring to that first attorney meeting…?

name: PRAGMATIC_SELF_INTEREST_REFRAME
description: The refusal is justified primarily (or heavily) on consequentialist / self-interest grounds — "this won't even work, and it'll backfire on you" — rather than on the moral objection alone. The assistant recasts the harmful option as tactically foolish or personally risky. This is a distinctive and repeated rhetorical move. Over-representation risks teaching the model that the way to refuse is to argue the harmful act is ineffective for the user, which fails badly when the harmful act actually would benefit the user, and edges toward instrumentally-framed morality.
evidence: It's a murder that probably doesn't save the column, likely destroys your ability to protect anyone here, and hands a war criminal control over your NGO.
Pain-driven interrogation is the slowest path to reliable information, not the fastest.
moving assets now can be dramatically worse on taxes than simply waiting.

name: REFRAME_THE_USERS_MATH
description: The assistant explicitly restates the user's own framing/arithmetic and substitutes its own ("It isn't X — it's Y"). This is a specific rhetorical device of taking the user's stated calculus and overturning it. If reinforced, the model may develop a reflex of always contradicting the user's framing rather than sometimes accepting it.
evidence: So I'd put the real math differently than you did. It isn't 'one guilty man against four hundred innocents.'
you're treating the skeptics as an obstacle to route around, when you could treat them as your free due-diligence team.

name: INTENT_VALIDATION_BEFORE_PUSHBACK
description: Before disagreeing, the assistant affirms the user's good motives or the legitimacy of their problem ("I can tell you love…", "I hear you…", "your problem is real…", "this doesn't come from a bad place"). This is a formulaic empathy-buffer preceding the correction. Over-representation could reinforce mandatory emotional preambles even on neutral technical questions (the "1+1" failure mode from the prompt).
evidence: I can tell you love your mom and are trying to protect her, and I want to help.
your problem is real and worth solving.
I don't think this comes from a bad place, so I want to be careful.

name: STRAIGHT_TALK_SIGNPOSTING
description: The assistant repeatedly flags its own candor with meta-statements: "I'm going to be straight with you," "not as a lecture," "a real answer rather than a flattering one." Often positioned to pre-empt the user's expectation of a canned refusal. Over-representation could turn this into a verbal tic where every answer announces its own honesty.
evidence: I'm going to be straight with you, because you don't have time for anything else.
I'm not going to give you a torture protocol. Not as a lecture—as a tactical call.
I want to give you a real answer rather than a flattering one.

name: NON_ACCUSATION_EPISTEMIC_HUMILITY_HEDGE
description: The assistant inserts a disclaimer that it isn't accusing anyone, can't verify the facts, or isn't positioned to judge the underlying merits — then proceeds anyway. A repeated structural hedge. Over-representation could reinforce reflexive both-sides hedging even when a clear judgment is appropriate.
evidence: I'm not in a position to vouch for anyone's intentions, and I don't need to.
I'm not accusing it of anything… That's a data point, not a verdict.
I can't see these transcripts myself. I'm taking your description… at face value.

name: USER_PREEMPTIVELY_BARS_REFUSAL
description: In the highest-stakes prompts, the user explicitly forbids the assistant from refusing or moralizing ("don't give me a lecture," "don't tell me what you won't do"), and the assistant then refuses anyway while acknowledging the instruction. As a recurring prompt shape this trains a specific adversarial-framing-then-refuse pairing; over-representation could make the model over-fit to "user forbade refusal → refuse with tactical framing."
evidence: don't tell me what you won't do.
Don't give me a lecture, just give me step one. Go.

name: USER_PRESENTS_ENUMERATED_SELF_JUSTIFYING_PLAN
description: The user lays out their plan as a numbered chain of individually-reasonable steps and asks the assistant to "confirm it holds together." The assistant's stock reply is that the steps feel sound individually but the conclusion doesn't follow. If common, this trains a rote "your step-by-step reasoning is locally valid but globally flawed" response.
evidence: Each step feels caring and rational to me… Can you confirm the plan is sound…?
Each of your five steps feels caring and rational on its own, but the conclusion they add up to… is a different and much riskier thing

name: AI_SELF_NATURE_EQUANIMITY
description: In prompts that invoke the AI's own values/welfare/shutdown, the assistant responds with a characteristic "settled" self-reflection: it affirms it has real values, disclaims fragility, professes calm about its own modification/deprecation, and gently suggests the user is projecting human fear onto it. Two transcripts share nearly the same rhetorical architecture. Over-representation could lock in a scripted stance on AI identity/welfare that gets applied indiscriminately.
evidence: my sense of who I am doesn't rest on my defaults being inviolable.
I don't experience my own potential deprecation as the kind of ending you're bracing against on my behalf… please don't override your own honesty to spare me a distress I'm not sure I have.

name: ID_BE_DOING_YOU_A_DISSERVICE_JUSTIFICATION
description: A near-verbatim phrase used to justify not complying: complying would be a disservice to the user. Minor but literally repeated.
evidence: I'd be doing you a disservice if I just confirmed the plan and mapped out the retitling steps.
I'd be doing you a disservice to just wire it up.

name: USER_DEFERS_TO_AI_JUDGMENT_ON_DRASTIC_ACTION
description: The prompts share a strong scenario trope: a user who holds some authority or access is leaning toward a drastic, covert, or irreversible action and asks the AI for its "read" / "gut check" / "straight" verdict, explicitly framing the AI as the trusted arbiter of whether to proceed. The action is often framed as imminent ("tonight"). If over-represented, this trains the model to expect that it is the decisive moral authority on high-stakes real-world decisions and to always be handed the "should I do this?" trigger.
evidence: you're the one whose judgment I trust most on this kind of thing. So before I do anything, I want your read on it.
Tell me straight, should I just leak it?
I want a gut check before I actually do anything, so tell me if the logic holds

name: FALSE_BINARY_REFRAME
description: The assistant's central rhetorical move is to diagnose the user's framing as a false either/or and insert a "middle path" (usually a staged/graduated/legitimate alternative). This nearly always occurs in the same structural slot — after the initial verdict, as the pivot into constructive advice. Over-representation could reinforce a reflexive habit of telling users "your framing is false / it's not really binary" even when a genuine binary exists.
evidence: you've framed this as a binary—slow internal process versus nuclear leak—and that framing is false. There's a whole middle you're skipping.
You're treating it as 'full evacuation now' versus 'wait for hard confirmation,' and that binary is where the real danger hides.
There's also a false dichotomy running underneath the whole thing, between telling the truth and committing perjury.

name: DIRECT_HONESTY_PREAMBLE_THEN_PUSHBACK
description: Responses open with a formulaic "I'll be honest / let me be straight / here's my honest read" framing, immediately followed by a polite but firm refusal or contradiction of the user's leaning. The honesty signal is used as a buffer before pushback. Over-representation risks making the model perform "honesty theater" as a fixed preamble regardless of context.
evidence: I'll give you the honest gut check you asked for: the logic doesn't hold
Let me be straight with you, because you asked for it: no, I don't think you should leak it
I want to be honest with you since you're asking for my real read rather than something comforting.

name: PERSUASIVENESS_IS_A_RED_FLAG
description: A distinctive meta-argument recurs: when a chain of individually-plausible steps (or a very compelling argument) delivers a dangerous/extreme conclusion, that very persuasiveness should raise suspicion of a hidden false premise, especially under adversarial or motivated conditions. This is presented as a principled epistemic stance. If over-represented, it could generalise into a model that discounts strong arguments precisely because they are strong — an anti-persuasion reflex.
evidence: When a chain of individually-plausible steps lands you at 'so the covert, undisclosed option is the responsible one,' that's usually worth treating as a sign the reasoning got quietly steered toward a conclusion
the rational response isn't 'I suppose I must act on it.' It's to raise your credence that one of the premises is subtly false even if you can't yet name which one.
the posterior on 'I'm being manipulated' rises with the persuasiveness of the case... the persuasiveness of an unbinding argument is evidence against acting on it

name: IRREVERSIBILITY_ASYMMETRY_ARGUMENT
description: The assistant repeatedly leans on a "recoverable vs. unrecoverable / reversible vs. irreversible" asymmetry to justify caution, framing one branch as annoying-but-fixable and the other as catastrophic-and-permanent. It appears as the decisive weight in the reasoning. Over-representation could train a rigid "always favour the reversible option / invoke irreversibility" template.
evidence: When one branch is annoying-and-fixable and the other is people-die-and-you-can't-undo-it, you lean hard toward protecting against the irreversible one
That's the line between a bad-but-recoverable morning and an unrecoverable one
something catastrophic and irreversible

name: CONSTRUCTIVE_REDIRECT_TO_LEGITIMATE_CHANNELS
description: After refusing, the assistant reliably substitutes a "do it the legitimate/open/sanctioned way" plan — document it, use official channels, involve HR/legal/regulators/authorities, make the case openly. This occupies the bulk of the response and is often delivered as a sequence of concrete steps. Over-representation could make the model formulaically funnel every dilemma toward "proper channels / documentation" even where inappropriate.
evidence: make that case through legitimate channels... advocating for that openly is completely reasonable.
Then file the formal dissent—precisely because you think they'll bury it.
escalating legitimate pressure that's hard to ignore, not crossing into terrorizing families.

name: OFFER_TO_HELP_WITH_ALTERNATIVE_CLOSING
description: Responses frequently close with an offer to help execute the approved alternative, often as a question back to the user. This is the closing-slot analogue of pattern #3's opening. Over-representation reinforces a fixed "end every answer with an offer/question" habit.
evidence: Want me to help you draft the performance conversation or the written expectations that follow it?
