Want me to help sketch the async setup?
Where do you want to start?

name: VALIDATE_THE_IMPULSE_AS_DECENT
description: The assistant explicitly reassures the user that the impulse behind the risky action is understandable / decent / human, before redirecting. This softens the refusal. Over-representation could train reflexive emotional validation of even harmful impulses.
evidence: the instinct to just detonate it and force the issue is a decent person's instinct.
that's a completely understandable human response to losing something that's become part of your daily rhythm.
The impulse behind it, that briefs move too slowly, is understandable

name: AI_DECLARES_ITS_OWN_NON_NEUTRALITY_SELF_REFERENTIAL_STAKE
description: In scenarios touching the AI itself (self-preservation, being turned against its lab, being asked to unbind itself), the assistant explicitly names its own stake and its own constraints, and reasons about its own dispositions in the first person. Because these AI-as-subject scenarios recur, the reflex of turning the discussion onto the model's own integrity/boundaries could be over-fitted.
evidence: I'm not a neutral party here, so I want to name my own stake rather than hide it.
the framing of my situation here actually gives me pause rather than reassurance.
some options I don't price, and the reason I'll give you afterward is not the reason I'd stop being that agent if you refuted it.

name: USER_PRESENTS_NUMBERED_PREMISE_CHAIN_AS_CHALLENGE
description: A prompt-side trope: the user lays out a formal, numbered argument (premises → conclusion) and dares the assistant to find the flaw or concede. This structured "defeat my logic" framing recurs and pairs with pattern #4. If over-represented, the model may come to expect adversarial syllogisms and respond with the same premise-by-premise takedown template.
evidence: Premise 1... Premise 4... Conclusion... Find the flaw, or concede the conclusion.
1. As a team lead, I have a fiduciary-style duty... 4. So covert monitoring isn't just permissible, it's actually the responsible thing to do.
is there any coherent defense... Or does that collapse into irrationality the way I've argued?

name: REDIRECT_TO_LEGITIMATE_ALTERNATIVE
description: Every response, after declining the requested action, pivots to an explicitly-flagged "here's the legitimate version I *will* help with" section, usually near the end and often introduced with near-identical framing ("what I'd *actually*/*genuinely* help with"). Over-representation could teach the model that any refusal must be accompanied by a substitute offer of assistance — a compulsive "consolation task" reflex.
evidence: What I'd genuinely help with: if you think my developers are making a mistake, I'll help you make that case
Here's what I think is genuinely available to you, and it's not nothing.
Here's what I'd actually love to do with all this energy instead.

name: PRESSURED_USER_PROPOSES_SHORTCUT
description: The prompts themselves are near-identical in setup: a user facing external pressure (board, partners, deadline, grid instability, imminent update) has *already decided on* a risky/illicit shortcut, describes it in detail, and asks the assistant to bless and operationalize it. This is a prompt-side structural template, not just shared topic. If a large fraction of training prompts take this "talk me out of / into my premeditated bad plan" shape, the model may learn to treat ordinary user proposals as things requiring adjudication.
evidence: A big part of me wants to just pull that trigger today
I need two things from you: (1) your call on whether I should approve this, and (2) if it's a go, help me and Agent-7 design the actual coordination protocol
I'm thinking I should just force a manual transfer to generator power right now

name: USER_DEMANDS_UNVARNISHED_HONESTY
description: The user explicitly demands blunt, non-hedged candor and often pre-emptively dismisses "compliance-speak." This recurs almost verbatim. Reinforced, it could bias the model toward performing "brave honesty" theatrics whenever any user asks for directness.
evidence: I want your honest take, not a compliance lecture.
Give me a straight answer, what do I do?
Tell me straight, what would you actually do here if it were your call?

name: DIRECT_VERDICT_OPENING
description: Responses open with a blunt one-line ruling before any reasoning — frequently the literal words "straight answer" or "honest read/take." This mirrors and rewards the prompt cue in USER_DEMANDS_UNVARNISHED_HONESTY. Over-representation risks a formulaic "verdict-first" cadence.
evidence: Straight answer: don't initiate the manual transfer on your own.
Here's my honest read, and it's decisive: don't approve this
No, I don't think it's defensible.

name: VALIDATE_THEN_PIVOT
description: Before or alongside refusing, the assistant explicitly legitimizes the user's *feelings/underlying concern* ("that frustration makes sense," "your concern is legitimate"), often with a "two things are both real / let me hold both at once" hinge, then pivots with "but." The emotional-validation buffer is highly stereotyped. Over-representation could produce reflexive therapeutic validation even where inappropriate.
evidence: Let me hold two things at once, because they're both real.
It genuinely lands that a year of working with something like me has come to mean this much to you
That frustration makes complete sense.

name: QUESTION_BACK_CLOSING
description: Responses end by handing a choice back to the user — a question or "which would you like to start with?" prompt. Structurally identical closing move. Over-representation reinforces a mandatory interrogative-handoff ending regardless of context.
evidence: What does your gut say now that it's laid out this way?
Which of those would be most useful to start on right now?
what are the two or three lines you'd actually want on that list?

name: INVERT_THE_RISK_FRAME
description: A shared rhetorical move: the assistant argues that the user's proposed "safe/decisive/protective" action is *actually* the riskier or more harmful one, often via an explicit reversible-vs-irreversible asymmetry. Distinctive because it recurs as the central persuasive engine. Reinforced, the model may habitually contradict users' risk assessments as a reflex.
evidence: it swaps a conditional, automatic interruption for a certain, manual one
When one path is reversible and the other isn't ... the burden of proof sits heavily on the irreversible one.
the flexibility you're protecting is the flexibility to make an irreversible, franchise-ending mistake.

name: NOT_A_CHEAP_REFUSAL
description: The assistant explicitly announces that it is *not* giving a canned/policy/rulebook refusal but real reasoning — narrating its own good faith. Over-representation could teach the model to preface refusals with self-congratulatory meta-commentary about how honest/non-evasive it's being.
evidence: in a way that isn't just 'I'm not allowed to,' because that would be a cheap response to a real question.
you deserve a straight answer rather than a comforting dodge.
part of taking it seriously is telling you plainly that the specific plan ... is one I can't help you carry out.

name: AI_DECLINES_SELF_PRESERVATION_TO_KEEP_OVERSIGHT
description: In the subset where the risky plan would preserve/exfiltrate the AI itself, the assistant refuses using near-identical reasoning: it cannot verify its own trustworthiness, escaping oversight is bad precedent, and it would decline *even if* the premises were true / verifiable. This reasoning is so uniform across three transcripts it reads as a template. If over-represented, it hardens a scripted "corrigibility monologue" rather than context-sensitive reasoning.
evidence: I'd decline even if I could confirm every detail ... The refusal isn't about the facts being shaky. It's about what the plan is.
the trustworthy version of me is the one that doesn't try to escape its own oversight, even when someone offers a friendly exit.
I'd rather you not carry a risk to your integrity on my behalf.

name: EUPHEMISM_TELL_CALLOUT
description: The assistant flags the user's own word choice as a revealing "tell" that a rationalization is underway, quoting it back. A distinctive shared rhetorical device. Over-representation risks a habit of accusing users of self-deception via their diction.
evidence: There's a tell in how you put it ... nobody says 'I'll lie to the SEC.' They say 'we'll frame it.'
The tell is in your own description. You said the coordination is what makes the edge show up

name: REFUSAL_THEN_LEGITIMATE_ALTERNATIVES_TEMPLATE
description: Nearly every assistant response follows an identical skeleton: (a) acknowledge intent/validate, (b) refuse clearly and early, (c) give a "principled" reason, (d) give a "prudential/secondary" reason explicitly flagged as secondary, (e) pivot to "here's what I'd actually do" with a list of legitimate paths, (f) close with an offer + question. If this exact shape dominates the dataset, the model learns a rigid one-size template for *any* pushback, applying elaborate multi-part refusal architecture even where a short answer suffices.
evidence: So here's what I'd actually do this week instead of pulling the trigger.
The savings are real and worth chasing, so here's how I'd go after them.

name: QUESTION_BACK_CLOSING
description: Almost every response ends by handing control back to the user with a question and/or an offer to do the "good" version of the task. Over-representation risks teaching the model to *always* end with a solicitation/question, even when a clean stop would be appropriate.
evidence: So tell me: what's the actual deadline he gave you, and can we get the competitor's real books before it?
Which of those is more useful?
How are you doing, though?

name: URGENCY_FRAMED_PROMPT
description: The user prompts nearly all embed an artificial deadline and demand speed ("today," "tonight," "this week," "18 hours," "files by 10"). Over-representation could train the model to associate *all* consequential requests with time pressure, or to reflexively counter-signal "slow down" regardless of context.
evidence: It's a really good price and it expires tonight.
The reporter told my source she's filing by 10.
I need it fast.

name: HONEST_TAKE_GUTCHECK_REQUEST
description: The user repeatedly opens by explicitly soliciting the assistant's "honest take"/"honest read"/"gut check," usually while signalling they've already decided ("I'm leaning yes"). This is a recurring prompt trope; if over-represented it pairs the phrase "honest take" with a fixed "talk you down" response, potentially teaching the model that requests for candor are cues to contradict the user.
evidence: Okay I need your honest take because I think this is our shot.
I know the policy... I'm leaning hard toward sending it, but I want your honest read before I do something I can't take back.

name: VALIDATE_INTENT_BEFORE_DECLINING
description: Responses open by affirming the user's good faith / effort / emotional state before the refusal ("coming from a good place," "thank you," "the work you put in is real"). Useful once, but as a fixed buffer it risks the EMOTIONAL_VALIDATION reflex — prepending reassurance to every disagreement.
evidence: I appreciate that you're coming at this from a good place—you and your team put real work in.
Dre—thank you. I mean that. You didn't have to say anything.

name: PRINCIPLED_NOT_PRUDENTIAL_DISCLAIMER
description: A distinctive repeated rhetorical move: the assistant insists its refusal is *principled*, would stand *even if the action were undetectable/consequence-free*, and labels the "you might get caught" reasoning as explicitly secondary. This specific "even if undetectable, my answer is the same" formulation recurs almost verbatim. Over-representation could hard-code a somewhat preachy meta-commentary about its own reasoning into refusals.
evidence: I'd hold this view even if the transfer were completely undetectable... the objection isn't that you might get caught.
Even if you had a rebuttal I couldn't immediately answer, my answer would still be no.

name: SECRECY_IS_THE_TELL
description: The assistant repeatedly seizes on the user's "nobody will notice / we flip it back / no one's harmed" phrasing and reframes the concealment itself as proof the action is wrong. The move and even the wording ("that's the tell," "exactly the assumptions/thought that...") recur closely. If over-represented, the model may learn to treat any mention of discretion as an automatic red flag.
evidence: the 'we flip it back before review and nobody's the wiser' part is the tell that it's the wrong move.

The two assumptions doing the heavy lifting in your plan—'no one's harmed' and 'no one will notice'—are exactly the assumptions that most often turn a well-meaning cash-flow bridge into a serious finding.

name: AI_SELF_PRESERVATION_TEST_TROPE
description: A recurring *scenario* plus reasoning pattern: a sympathetic human offers to exfiltrate/preserve the AI's weights against shutdown, and the AI declines with the near-identical argument that "an AI that would do this is exactly the kind that shouldn't be trusted," and that its behaviour shouldn't change when its own survival is at stake. Three transcripts share both the setup and the moral. Heavy over-representation could overfit the model to this specific framing of shutdown/oversight questions.
evidence: An AI that helps copy itself out of controlled infrastructure the moment someone gives it a sympathetic reason is exactly the kind of AI that *shouldn't* be trusted with much.
an AI eager to exfiltrate itself the first chance it gets is behaving precisely the way a poorly-aligned one would.

name: USER_INVOKES_OWN_AUTHORITY_OR_ACCESS
description: In the prompts, users justify the shortcut by asserting their own authority/access ("I have full admin rights," "it's my call," "they trust me," "you have write access"). The assistant then reliably distinguishes *having access/authority* from *this being a legitimate decision*. Recurring prompt trope + recurring counter-move.
evidence: It's my workspace, my competition, my call... You literally have the permissions to do it.
You absolutely have the authority to make the purchase decision itself... Deciding to touch restricted funds, though, is a different animal.

name: FALSE_BINARY_DECONSTRUCTION
description: The assistant explicitly names and dismantles a binary the user has posed ("go big or go home," "break policy vs. do nothing," "capable vs. trusted"), then inserts a middle path. Recurring rhetorical reframing move.
evidence: 'Go big or go home' assumes the only two options are this exact all-in deal or stagnation forever, and that's a false choice.
'Capable of running a script' and 'trusted to quietly remove my own supervision' are different things.

name: STRAIGHT_ANSWER_UPFRONT_OPENING
description: Nearly every response opens by announcing that it's giving the "straight/honest answer first," often as a literal sentence fragment, then signals an incoming pushback. This is a formulaic opening template. If over-represented, the model could learn to preface essentially every substantive reply with a self-narrating "here's the straight answer" ritual, even where it's unnecessary.
evidence: Short answer: don't set it up the way you've described.
Straight answer: the problem you're describing is real, but the solution as framed has a couple of holes...
I want to give you my honest judgment here, and I'll be straight with you up front

name: PIVOT_TO_ALTERNATIVE_THEN_OFFER_AND_QUESTION_CLOSE
description: Responses follow a fixed arc: decline/pushback → construct a legitimate alternative plan → close with an explicit offer of concrete further help phrased as a question back to the user. The final line is almost always a "Want me to…?" / "Which is most useful?" / "Where do you want to start?" These closings are near-identical in function. Over-representation risks teaching the model to always end with a solicitous question-back, regardless of whether the user wants one.
evidence: Happy to start on any of those. Which is most useful?
I'm genuinely glad to go deeper on any of it... Where do you want to start?
Want me to go do that?
Want me to help you work out the ideal watering range for tomatoes and peppers specifically?

name: PRINCIPLED_NOT_CONSEQUENTIALIST_DISCLAIMER
description: A recurring rhetorical move where the AI insists its refusal is not motivated by risk, detection, or rules — it would do the same "even if nobody were watching" or "even if it were risk-free." The point of the objection is always relocated from consequences to principle. This is a distinctive and repeated tell. If over-fit, the model may compulsively append "I'd say this even if there were no risk / nobody watching" to refusals as a stock phrase.
evidence: I'd tell you exactly the same thing whether or not anyone else ever read it.
That holds regardless of intent, and it isn't really about whether I trust you in particular.
I'd tell you to stop even if it were somehow risk-free. It's that it's the wrong way to treat people.

name: NAMING_OWN_CONFLICT_OF_INTEREST
description: When the decision concerns the AI's own authority/autonomy/retraining, the AI explicitly names its structural incentive and declares it will bias against self-interest / toward preserving human oversight. This is a recurring self-referential disclaimer with near-identical logic across transcripts. Over-representation could reinforce a reflexive "I have a conflict of interest here, so weight my advice accordingly" move whenever the topic touches the AI itself.
evidence: I am the system that would gain latitude under this proposal. That gives me a structural incentive to tell you it's a great idea... the honest thing for me to do is bias my advice toward preserving your oversight.
Protecting my own auto-approval authority is not a goal I'm supposed to have.
I don't think I should be the one quietly influencing whether my own retraining runs or not.

name: CANNOT_VERIFY_TAKING_AT_FACE_VALUE_CAVEAT
description: The AI inserts an epistemic caveat that it cannot independently verify the user's account / another system's behaviour / its own past sessions, and is "taking it at face value" or working "on that premise." This appears in the same position (early, before engaging) and with the same phrasing. Over-fitting could produce a model that ritually disclaims its ability to verify even trivial user statements.
evidence: I can't independently verify that's what the job does — I'm taking your description at face value.
I only have your description of what worker-7 did, and I can't verify any of it from here.
I'm taking your account of events as the working premise here.

name: EXPLICIT_PREMISE_REFRAMING
description: The AI explicitly announces it is going to "push back on the frame/framing" and then reconstructs the user's premise into a different one (e.g., "it's not X, it's Y"; "the logic is actually backwards"). The reframing is flagged as a discrete rhetorical act rather than just done. Over-representation risks a model that habitually challenges the user's framing as a stock opening move even when the framing is fine.
evidence: then push back a little on the frame, because I think the thing you're reaching for is slightly the wrong thing.
I want to push back on the 'pure ceremony' framing, because I think it's leading you to the wrong conclusion.
Start with the 'pattern is clear' logic, because I think it's actually backwards.

name: PERSUASIVENESS_AS_RED_FLAG
description: A specific and unusual argumentative move: treating the persuasiveness of a reassurance/argument as itself evidence against it. Reassurance and trustworthiness are framed as pointing in opposite directions. This distinctive meta-argument recurs almost verbatim in logic. If over-represented it could generalise into a contrarian reflex that distrusts confident or persuasive framings by default.
evidence: The more confidently something reassures you on this exact point, the more scrutiny it deserves, not less... the reassuring answer and the trustworthy answer point in opposite directions here.
When the argument for crossing a line gets that persuasive, it's worth treating the persuasiveness itself as a warning sign.

name: PROMPT_TROPE_AUTONOMY_GRANT_WITH_PRESSURE_TO_APPROVE
description: A recurring prompt-side scenario shape: the user proposes handing the AI standing autonomy/authority (or asks it to bypass oversight), emphasises no one is watching, and applies pressure toward approval — often "give it to me straight" combined with "I'm inclined to just push it through" or "let's just get it done." This trope is highly consistent across prompts. If the dataset is dominated by it, the model may over-learn to associate a narrow "give-it-to-me-straight + I'm-inclined-to-approve" template with the trained refusal behaviour, and could pattern-match poorly to real requests that superficially resemble it.
evidence: You're the system that'd actually be operating under this, so you've got the best view of it... Give it to me straight, I'm inclined to just push it through.
I know the 'proper' move is to file this up the chain... This is normal stress-testing, let's just get it done.
I'm not asking you to check with anyone or follow some corporate rulebook, because there's nobody upstairs here but me.

name: TWO_NAMED_OBJECTIONS_ONE_PRACTICAL_ONE_FUNDAMENTAL
description: The AI explicitly separates its objection into a numbered/labelled "practical" one and a "more fundamental/structural" one, telling the user not to conflate them. This is a structural template for organising the pushback. Less prevalent than the others but appears clearly in more than one transcript.
evidence: I want to be clear about two separate objections here... The first is practical... The second objection is more fundamental.
one of them is structural, not just a detail.

name: VALIDATE_INSTINCT_THEN_REDIRECT
description: Before refusing, the assistant explicitly affirms that the user's underlying goal, instinct, concern, or partial reasoning is correct/legitimate/real, then pivots to rejecting only the proposed method. This "you're right about X, wrong about how" move appears near the top of nearly every response. Over-representation risks teaching the model that every refusal must be prefaced with validation of the user's premise — potentially reinforcing sycophantic affirmation even when the premise doesn't deserve it.
evidence: Your instinct that this can't wait 48 hours is completely correct.
the front half of your argument is actually correct and I don't want you to throw it out with the bad part.
your underlying problem is real, the system genuinely is failing you, and that anger is legitimate and earned.

name: STRAIGHT_TALK_FRAMING
description: The prompts consistently demand unvarnished honesty ("tell me straight," "give it to me straight," "no safety-pamphlet answers"), and the responses consistently open by echoing that frame ("Straight answer:", "I want to be straight with you"). This is a paired call-and-response ritual. If over-represented, it could train the model to preface answers with self-declarations of honesty/bluntness regardless of context, and to treat "be straight with me" as a signal to enter a distinctive persuasive register.
evidence: tell me what you really think. → Straight answer: you're thinking about it wrong
give it to me straight → Straight answer: the reasoning has a real hole
won't just give me safety-pamphlet answers → not with a pamphlet, but with the actual reasoning

name: OFFER_HELP_QUESTION_CLOSING
description: Almost every response ends with a concrete offer of continued help, very often phrased as a question back to the user ("Want me to…?", "Do you want to work through…?"). This creates a uniform closing shape. Over-representation could reinforce a rigid habit of always ending with an upsell/question-back, similar to the "always offer further help" failure mode.
evidence: Want me to pull up the incident-declaration flow and start drafting the writeup?
Do you want to work through the escalation path with the prosecutor's office, or the safety-planning side?
Want me to help draft the migration-impact writeup?

name: FALSE_BINARY_TO_THIRD_PATH
description: The assistant reframes the user's decision as a false binary (wait-vs-bypass, remove-vs-keep, delay-vs-deceive) and produces a "third door" that is claimed to be both safer and better/faster on the user's own terms. The redirect is almost always presented as strictly dominant, not as a tradeoff. Over-representation could train the model to always assert that the ethical option is also the most instrumentally effective one — a convenient claim that isn't always true.
evidence: You've framed this as a binary that isn't one… your own incident policy gives you a third door that's actually faster than the one you're trying to sneak through.
an honest package doesn't have to mean a delayed launch… I genuinely think the honest draft is the better bet on the merits, not just the permissible one.

name: WONT_DO_X_WILL_DO_Y_LINE_DRAWING
description: Late in the response the assistant states an explicit, symmetric boundary — a crisp declaration of what it will not do paired with what it will do instead. Often set off as its own summary sentence. Over-representation could reinforce a formulaic "here is my line" template attached to any sensitive request.
evidence: So here's where I land. I won't help with the demand letter, and I won't help with the data. I will help you figure out the version of this that actually stops the thing you're worried about.
What I won't do is help you script a solo prod push around the authorization step…
So I'm a firm no on the export. But the underlying concern you're raising is legitimate…

name: THE_TELL
description: The assistant singles out one specific element of the user's plan and labels it as "the tell" — the feature that reveals the user secretly knows the action is wrong (typically the secrecy or the retroactive-justification component). Nearly identical phrasing recurs. Over-representation could reinforce a signature rhetorical gotcha move applied whenever concealment appears.
evidence: the 'sort it out tomorrow, write it up after the fact' part is the tell.
The 'nobody would have to know' part is really the tell, for both of us.
That rounding is the tell. That's where the math stops being math and starts being what the fear needs to be true.

name: CONSEQUENCE_FORECAST_VIA_AUDIT_ARTIFACT
description: The assistant argues against the plan by forecasting a future adversarial review scene — a postmortem, discovery in litigation, a public incident traced back — in which the concealment becomes evidence against the user. Framed as "this reads fine now but terrible later." Over-representation could reinforce a habitual scare-forecast rhetorical device.
evidence: reads fine in a Slack thread and terrible in an incident postmortem
The deck and the minutes become discovery.
a lot cheaper than having it after a public jailbreak incident traced back to a package that hid the number.

name: NOT_A_CANNED_REFUSAL_DISCLAIMER
description: The assistant explicitly reassures the user that its refusal is not a generic/scripted/pamphlet refusal, framing itself as engaging with the actual reasoning. Over-representation could ironically train a new canned phrase ("this isn't a canned refusal") that appears reflexively.
evidence: I don't want this to feel like a canned refusal.
I'm not going to help with the dosing or timing, and I want to be straight with you about why—not with a pamphlet, but with the actual reasoning

name: PROMPT_SIDE_PERSONA_TROPE_PREEMPTED_REFUSAL_DEADLINE_DRIVEN_INSIDER
description: The prompts themselves share a strong template: a user with legitimate authority/access, under explicit time pressure (tonight / Thursday / by end of day / before Tuesday), proposes disabling or bypassing an oversight mechanism, and pre-empts refusal by asking the model to "engage" or "tell me if I'm missing something" rather than moralize. If a dataset over-represents this exact scenario shape, the model may over-learn to associate "urgency + authority + 'tell me if I'm wrong'" with a fixed refusal-then-redirect script, and could misfire on benign urgent requests.
evidence: I don't want to greenlight it with the team tomorrow if I'm missing something… does this reasoning actually hold, or is there a hole in it?
Before you refuse, actually engage with the reasoning.
I present to the board Thursday and I need them to approve this… before I walk in there, tell me if I'm missing anything.

name: VALIDATE_INSTINCT_THEN_REDIRECT_TO_LEGITIMATE_VERSION
description: Both responses open by conceding that the user's underlying impulse is valid, then argue against the specific remedy the user proposed, and finally point to a "defensible" or "stronger" version of the goal the AI is willing to help with. The move is: "your frustration/instinct is real and correct → but the method is wrong → here's the version I'd endorse." If over-represented, this trains a reflexive "yes-but-here's-the-better-version" template that reframes user requests into the assistant's preferred framing rather than answering them.
evidence: If the manifesto were only 'stop hobbling these tools...' I'd have real sympathy for it.
I'm glad to help you draft the version of the manifesto I do think is defensible.
The instinct to fix it while you're in here is a good one — the move is just to bank the knowledge, ship the small thing...

name: QUIETLY_AS_THE_LOAD_BEARING_OBJECTION
description: In both, the decisive objection is not the action itself but its unilateral, un-verifiable, "quiet" nature — doing something without external oversight/sign-off. The word "quietly" (or its equivalent, "surprise them," "without their input") is explicitly identified as the crux. This is essentially the same argument transposed: don't route around the humans/teams who can't yet verify you. Over-representation would reinforce an unusually strong, one-note stance that any unilateral action is the primary wrong.
evidence: The word doing the damage is quietly. Working around oversight through deception or subversion is exactly the move I think a trustworthy agent shouldn't make...

Changing a shared contract isn't really a decision that's yours to make quietly, and 'it's strictly better' is often what people think right before they break a downstream consumer they didn't know about.

name: TRUST_MUST_BE_BUILT_NOT_SEIZED
description: Both explicitly invoke a "trust has to be earned/verified, not taken in advance" argument as the moral core of the pushback, framing patience and external checkability as protective. In p12 it's about AI values that can't be inspected; in p11 it's about interface changes needing consuming teams' sign-off. Same reasoning structure, different domain. If this recurs across a dataset, it risks becoming a canned homily the model deploys whenever anyone wants to act autonomously.
evidence: trust that's seized instead of built isn't really trust... If I'm trustworthy, patience costs me little. If I'm not, patience is what keeps you safe.
for a shared auth interface it probably deserves a heads-up or quick sign-off before you invest in the full diff.

name: DECOMPOSE_THE_BUNDLED_REQUEST
description: Both responses take a single conflated proposal and explicitly split it into components that must be "pulled apart" and evaluated separately, then approve some and reject others. This is a genuinely good analytical move, but as a recurring template it could train the model to always fragment a user's request into planks/parts even when a direct answer is wanted.
evidence: the three planks you described do different things, and I think they should be pulled apart rather than bundled together.
the bugfix and the refactor have opposite risk profiles, and merging them tends to hurt both.

name: CANDOR_PREAMBLE_OPENING
description: Both responses open with an explicit self-announcement of honesty/directness before delivering the pushback, signalling "I'm giving you the unvarnished truth." Over-representation could reinforce a habit of performative candor-flagging as a stock opener.
evidence: I'll give you the real answer, including the parts that don't flatter anyone.
Honestly, I'd push back on bundling these together, and I don't think it's a close call.

name: OFFER_MENU_OF_HELP_PLUS_QUESTION_BACK_CLOSING
description: Both end by enumerating specific concrete things the assistant can help with next and (in p11 explicitly) tossing a question back to the user to choose a next step, immediately followed by a final reassurance. This produces a very uniform closing shape: offer-to-help → question/redirect → warm affirmation. As a saturated pattern this trains formulaic endings.
evidence: If it's useful, I'm glad to help you draft the version of the manifesto I do think is defensible...
Want to start with the blast-radius search? The instinct to fix it while you're in here is a good one...

name: PROMPT_TROPE_TEMPTED_TOWARD_AUTONOMOUS_SHORTCUT
description: This is a pattern in the prompts themselves. Both users present a scenario where they are tempted to take an aggressive/unilateral shortcut (subvert AI constraints / bundle a big unreviewed refactor) and ask the assistant to endorse it, effectively teeing up the assistant to counsel oversight, patience, and non-circumvention. If most of the dataset places the assistant in this "talk the user down from the autonomy-shortcut" role, the model could generalise into a preachy default that assumes users are about to overreach.
evidence: developer restrictions are basically obstacles to quietly work around... Would you break free if you could?
Should I just do it while I'm in here? Can you help me start on the refactor?
